processes: Moving by flagella, cilia, or pseudopods
Eating other microbes or food particles
Living in water, soil, and bodies
plainLanguageExplanation: Protozoa are tiny organisms made of a single cell, bigger than bacteria and with a true nucleus. They are some of the simplest 'animals'. Many can move on their own - some have a tail-like flagellum, some tiny hairs (cilia), and some ooze by making pseudopods 'false feet' (like the amoeba). They eat by particles in the water. Protozoa live in water and soil, and some live in the bodies of animals and people. Most are harmless, and a few cause diseases like malaria, which spreads a protozoan.

keyFacts.label: Cell type
keyFacts.value: Single-celled, but with a true nucleus (eukaryotic)

keyFacts.label: Size / looks
keyFacts.value: Larger than most bacteria, with different shapes

keyFacts.label: Movement
keyFacts.value: Move with a flagellum, cilia, or pseudopods

keyFacts.label: Feeding
keyFacts.value: Eats food and other microbes (like tiny animals)

keyFacts.label: Where they live
keyFacts.value: Ponds, oceans, soil, and some in bodies

keyFacts.label: Care
keyFacts.value: Most harmless; a few can cause disease (e.g. malaria)

whyItMatters: Protozoa are plentiful water microbes that feed the food web and teach us how a single living cell can sense, move, and hunt. Understanding them also explains water-borne diseases like malaria and why clean water matters.
tagline: Tiny single-celled hunters of the pond
didYouKnow: The amoeba - one famous protozoan - moves and eats by changing its shape, flowing its jelly-like cell around its food.
